proof_summary: Using the Euclid–Euler form, write an even perfect number as \(n=2^kq\), where \(q=2^{k+1}-1\) is prime.  The proper divisors contain the disjoint families \(1,2,\ldots,2^k\) and \(q,2q,\ldots,2^{k-1}q\), so binary expansions of the quotient and remainder modulo \(q\) represent every integer below \(n\) as a subset sum; perfectness represents \(n\) itself and bounds all subset sums by \(n\), making the attainable sums exactly \(0,\ldots,n\).
